title: China’s External Surplus Makes a “Mandarin Accord” Inevitable
gist: Jim O'Neill argues that a Plaza Accord-style currency agreement aimed at China — a 'Mandarin Accord' — has become increasingly necessary and is effectively inevitable, because China's external surplus and undervalued currency cannot be sustained indefinitely.

insights.claim: A new multilateral currency agreement to address today's global imbalances has become increasingly necessary, with the 1985 Plaza Accord — in which the US and four major trading partners coordinated to weaken the dollar — as the direct precedent.
insights.speaker: Jim O'Neill
insights.so_what: A coordinated-devaluation-style accord would be a regime change for FX: position for renminbi appreciation and dollar weakness if policy talk shifts that way.
insights.quote: As with the Plaza Accord in 1985, when the United States and four of its major trading partners agreed to coordinate policies to weaken the US dollar, a new agreement to address today’s global imbalances has become increasingly necessary.
insights.locator: LONDON—In keeping with the adage that history never repeats itself

insights.claim: China's currency is undervalued and its external surplus is the source of today's global imbalances, which is why the current configuration cannot persist indefinitely.
insights.speaker: Jim O'Neill
insights.so_what: Implies asymmetric upside risk in CNY and downside risk for exporters and sectors reliant on a cheap renminbi.
insights.quote: Given China’s undervalued currency, the situation simply cannot be sustained indefinitely.
insights.locator: As with the Plaza Accord in 1985

insights.claim: Developments in international macroeconomic policy with clear historical precedents could arrive soon, on the view that history rhymes rather than repeats.
insights.speaker: Jim O'Neill
insights.so_what: Sets a near-term watch item: signs of US-China policy coordination on currency would be a tradable macro catalyst.
insights.quote: I suspect that we could soon see developments in international macroeconomic policy for which there are clear precedents
